hook.text: A toddler calls every round object "ball." The moon, an orange, a doorknob—all "ball."

buildup.text: This is overextension: stretching a known word to cover things the child hasn't labeled yet.

discovery.text: Children overextend based on shape more than color, size, or texture. Shape dominates early categories.

twist.text: They often know the categories are different. Overextension is a vocabulary gap, not a concept gap.

climax.text: As vocabulary grows, the boundaries tighten and "ball" shrinks back to actual balls.

punchline.text: They know more than they can say.

quiz.question: Why do children overextend words like 'ball'?
options: They lack vocabulary for other round objects
They truly think all round things are balls

details.summary: Young children overextend words by applying them too broadly: calling all four-legged animals doggy or all round objects ball. Overextension reveals how children's early categories are organized around perceptual similarity before being refined by feedback and expanding knowledge.
details.whyItMatters: Overextension is not error but evidence of active categorization. It shows children testing hypotheses about word meaning and adjusting as they learn more.
takeaways: Children apply words to perceptually similar non-members
Overextension is most common between 12 and 30 months
It reveals how early categories are organized by appearance

faq.question: Why do children overextend rather than underextend?
faq.answer: Children encounter many objects they do not yet have words for, so they stretch existing words to fill gaps. Calling a horse doggy works communicatively even if inaccurate. Overextension is partly a production strategy, using known words when the right one is unavailable.

faq.question: When does overextension stop?
faq.answer: Overextension declines sharply between ages two and three as vocabulary expands and corrective feedback accumulates. As children learn more words, they no longer need to stretch existing ones. Occasional overextension persists in unfamiliar domains even in adults.
